newsitem.title: CHINA: INTERVIEW-Asia currency fallout to last three years.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Asia currency fallout to last three years.

text.p: Asian nations hit by currency turmoil face at least three years of resulting economic adjustment, Ken Davies, senior regional economist with the Economist Intelligence Unit told Reuters on Tuesday.
The arrival of contagious currency speculation signalled the end to years of profligate spending and cheap loans that inflated economies throughout this fast- growing region, he said.
"The problem is overcapacity throughout the region," Davies said. "It will take some time to work its way out."

Davies warned that there was as yet no end in sight for the turmoil hitting Asia's four most volatile currencies -- the Malaysian ringgit, the Indonesian rupiah, the Thai baht and the Philippine peso.
In the past two weeks the baht and peso were both floated and effectively devalued. Markets were quiet on Tuesday but the ringgit and rupiah were both considered vulnerable to attack.
More "managed devaluations" or depreciations were possible, but they would not erode economic growth rates to below those of developed nations, Davies said.

"We're going through a business cycle," he said. "People don't expect this region to do that, they expect straight line growth. But you do periodically get downturns, and overcapacity has to be dealt with in various harsh ways."
He urged affected nations to confront some of the systemic flaws that prompted the currency chaos.
"The worst scenario would be some sort of retreat from convertibility, a refusal to face the facts," he said.
Davies argued that, rather than closing the gates to ward off capital flows blamed for the recent volatility, the region should instead be seeking greater openness.
Closing capital accounts and instituting foreign exchange controls were short- term measures that assisted stability when currency speculators were perched on the doorstep, he said.
But they were a longer-term hazard, preventing the free-flow of capital and eroding competitiveness by encouraging the production of outmoded products that became stockpiled, he added.
"It's really a question of opening up to higher tech in an appropriate way," Davies said.

"What countries really need to do is build basic physical and human infrastructure. If people are not healthy, not properly trained, if they don't actually have the capacity for personal growth and being independent, then a country is unlikely to fulfill its true potential."

Davies supported the introduction of better regulation through, for example, an Asian equivalent of the Bank for International Settlements or the sort of regional clearing system promoted by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, AsiaClear.
But he warned that in order for all regulation to be effective and for regional financial infrastructure to improve, national financial systems must also be effective.
"Very often it is a question of political system. If you have a hugely corrupt elite you will have difficulty attaining international standards," he said.

Stressing that he was not specifically referring to Thailand, but also to documented events in Japan, South Korea and China, Davies said no regional regulatory system would work until the national financial system was effectively managed.
"It's quite a serious problem. Really it's a question of political reform," he said. "But it's a good idea to have standards set out and agreed."
